// pre-release, built in the open

Safe at any speed.

Jet is a memory-safe compiled language with a beginner-first surface and explicit expert controls. The compiler checks source before producing native code. Examples show the language's current supported path without promising production readiness.

Install jet Read the tour

The example gives two readings of one program; the source and current checks define what is supported.

hero.jet 
// hero.jet is a complete program. Run it: jet run hero.jet
fn plan(dest: String, seats: Int{2}) String -> "{dest}, party of {seats}"
          └ default rides the type: plan("Lisbon") seats 2
fn load_port() Int !IOError -> Ok(8080)
             └ the whole failure contract, in the signature
fn run() {
      └ inferred effect row -[IO]>: this program prints
    port :: load_port() ?? 3000
                        └ ?? discharges the failure or it propagates
    print(plan("Lisbon", 3))
    print("listening on {port}")
}
  • The example fits in one file, with no project setup shown.
  • :: binds a value. Strings fill in {name} slots themselves.
  • If load_port fails with no fallback, the program reports the error and exits 1.
  • Effects are typed. run() infers -[IO]>; declare a row to cap what a function may touch.
  • Failure is part of the signature. !IOError is the entire contract; unchecked exceptions do not exist.
  • Safety facts are explicit at the sites where expert controls are used.
$ jet run hero.jet
Lisbon, party of 3
listening on 8080

// the deal

No footguns. Not hidden. Gone.

Memory safety and type safety are never configurable. Undefined behavior is not a beginner mistake you learn to avoid; in Jet it is structurally out of reach until an expert asks for it in writing.

Footguns are opt-in

When you need raw memory or exact layout, the escape hatch exists, and it signs its name. Every unsafe region carries a written reason, at the site, on the record.

#Unsafe("read a device register") {
    // audited, on the record
}

A documented form for each operation

The examples use one documented form for each operation, so the syntax stays visible.

examples/features/basics/pattern_matching.jet
if c == {
    .Active(id) | .Reconnecting(id) -> { return "live:{id}" }
    .Idle(_) -> { return "idle" }
    .Closed -> return "closed"
    else -> return "unknown"
}

Errors are part of the product

Every diagnostic has a registered code, a what, a why, and a fix, and its text is snapshot-tested like any feature. This one is real:

Error [E0112]: `plan` wants Int (a whole number) for argument 2, but this is String (text) --> broken.jet:4:26 | 4 | print(plan("Lisbon", "three")) | ^^^^^^^ Why: every argument must match its parameter's type Fix: use Int (a whole number) here More: jet-lang.dev/e/E0112

// proof over promises

The examples are the spec.

Feature examples are runnable corpus files with golden-tested output. This page names the source files and labels the outputs shown here; the golden harness catches drift in those examples.

Defaults ride the type

A default value lives on the type, and it may name an earlier parameter. Call box_dims(4) and get a cube.

cube.jetfrom examples/features/basics/default_refs.jet
fn box_dims(w: Int, h: Int{w}, d: Int{h}) String -> "{w}x{h}x{d}"

fn run() {
    print(box_dims(4))
    print(box_dims(4, 2))
    print(box_dims(4, 2, 1))
}
$ jet run cube.jet
4x4x4
4x2x2
4x2x1

Explicit task lifetimes

The example shows explicit join, all, race, any, and detach handling for spawned tasks.

examples/features/concurrency/tasks_join_all.jet
joined :: task work(5)
print(joined.join() ?? panic("join failed"))

results :: task.all {work(1), work(2), work(3)} ?? panic("task.all failed")
print(results[0] + results[1] + results[2])

// web target example

A web target, still a checked subset.

The site presents a web-widget example for the early jet build --target web target; broader browser/UI parity remains open.

widget/counter.jet, web-target example
widget/counter.jet
use core.ui as ui
use core.reactive as reactive
#[Target(Web), HTML("shell.html")]

fn run() {
    count :: reactive.signal(0)
    ui.reactive_render(() -> {
        n := count.get()
        color := "#2E2E33"
        if n % 2 == 1 -> color = "#E8232A"
        backend :: ui.null_backend()
        tree :: ui.box([
            ui.node_color("count: {n}", 160.0, 40.0, color),
            ui.button("Add one", on_click: () -> {
                count.set(count.get() + 1)
            })
        ])
        ui.mount(backend, tree, ui.constraint(0.0, 0.0, 300.0, 120.0))
    })
}

// jetpack

The environment is part of the program.

jetpack is Jet's environment engine. Projects declare tools in env.jet; jetpack env realizes the declared environment as a project shell.

Try a named tool. jetpack use can build an ephemeral shell for the packages you name; support remains subject to the current environment backend.

Builds record their inputs. jet build writes a receipt keyed by the sources, imports, and toolchain that went in, so unchanged work can be replayed.

$ jetpack env # enter the project's declared shell $ jetpack use ripgrep@nixpkgs -- rg --version # borrow a tool $ jetpack add ripgrep@nixpkgs # adopt it into env.jet $ jetpack hangar du # see what the store holds $ jet build # receipted; unchanged inputs replay

// start now

Start with a short command sequence.

# install (x86_64 Linux and macOS, via Nix) $ nix profile install github:jet-language/jet $ jet version
# first program $ jet new hello $ cd hello $ jet run hello, world

Jet is pre-release and changes weekly. Package workflows, Windows support, and stability guarantees remain under active development. If this site ever disagrees with the compiler, the compiler is right; jet explain knows more than any web page.
